answer.label: Not Confucius — from Laozi’s Tao Te Ching
answer.authorDates: fl. 6th c. BC (traditional, semi-legendary) · Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
answer.sourceLine: The line is chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching, ascribed to Laozi — not Confucius, to whom it is only “erroneously” credited. The literal Chinese, 千里之行始於足下, means “a journey of a thousand li starts beneath one’s feet”; the familiar “single step” wording comes from James Legge’s 1891 English translation.

source.excerpt: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
trail: Wikipedia states the saying is from “chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching, a foundational work of Taoism, ascribed to Laozi,” and is “also erroneously ascribed to his contemporary Confucius.”
Wikiquote lists the line under Laozi’s Tao Te Ching (ch. 64) and flags that it is often misattributed to Confucius.
James Legge’s 1891 translation reads “the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step” — the source of the modern “single step” wording.
The literal Chinese 千里之行始於足下 means a journey begins “beneath one’s feet”, not with a discrete “step.”
source.excerptNote: James Legge’s 1891 rendering of chapter 64. Modern retellings swap “li” for “miles” and “commenced” for “begins,” but the “single step” gloss is Legge’s.

source.rightsNote: The underlying text is the Tao Te Ching (ch. 64), a work of roughly the 4th–6th century BC. The familiar English “single step” wording descends from James Legge’s 1891 translation (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 39), published well before 1931 and in the public domain; the common modern paraphrase (“miles” for “li”) is an anonymous, unowned modernization of that public-domain rendering.

author.name: Laozi (Lao Tzu)
author.heading: About Laozi (Lao Tzu)
author.metaLine: fl. 6th c. BC (traditional) · Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Laozi (“Old Master”) is the semi-legendary figure to whom the Tao Te Ching, the foundational text of Taoism, is traditionally ascribed. Traditional accounts place him in the 6th century BC in the state of Chu, though many scholars regard the book as a composite work compiled somewhat later. He is a distinct figure from his rough contemporary Confucius, with whom the sayings of the Tao Te Ching are frequently confused.

misattribution.heading: Not Confucius
misattribution.intro: The line is a genuine, ancient Chinese saying — but it belongs to Laozi’s Tao Te Ching, not Confucius, and the tidy “single step” wording is a translator’s phrasing rather than a literal rendering.

items.why: Confucius (Kong Qiu) did not write this. Wikipedia notes the saying is “erroneously ascribed to his contemporary Confucius,” and Wikiquote lists it under Laozi while noting it is “often misattributed to Confucius.”
The literal Chinese, 千里之行始於足下, means the journey begins “beneath one’s feet.” The “single step” formulation entered English through James Legge’s 1891 translation.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is authentically ancient — chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching, ascribed to Laozi — but it is not Confucius, and the “single step” is Legge’s English, not the literal Chinese.

context.heading: A saying about small beginnings
lead: In chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching, the line sits in a series of images about how large things grow from tiny ones: a tree that fills the arms grew from a sprout, a nine-storey tower rose from a heap of earth, and a thousand-li journey begins under one’s feet. The point is Laozi’s philosophy of acting on things while they are still small and manageable.

Because Laozi and Confucius are the two most famous names of early Chinese thought and lived around the same era, feel-good aphorisms from either are routinely swapped — and this one is very often pinned on Confucius in English-language quote collections.
